about: Modern verified layer for Gibbon's Decline and Fall (1776–1789): his claims beside current scholarship. Interpretive questions (why Rome fell) are marked Refined with the main modern positions, not a single 'answer'.

entries.topic: Why the Western Roman Empire fell
match: natural and inevitable effect of immoderate greatness
I have described the triumph of barbarism and religion
entries.modern: Historians no longer give one cause. Three main positions: pressure from outside — the Huns driving Goths and others across the frontiers, then the loss of Africa's tax revenue to the Vandals in 439 (Heather); real material collapse in the West shown by archaeology — fewer coins, poorer pottery, smaller buildings and cattle after 400 (Ward-Perkins); and 'late antiquity' as a transformation rather than a fall, with the East thriving (Brown). Most agree the Western state failed while the Eastern one survived for a thousand years.
entries.value: Multi-causal; Western collapse c. 400–476, Eastern empire to 1453
sources: Peter Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire: A New History (2005)
Bryan Ward-Perkins, The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization (2005)
Peter Brown, The World of Late Antiquity (1971)
entries.relationship: Gibbon's 'immoderate greatness' — an empire too large to defend — survives in modern accounts of overstretched frontiers and armies; his weight on religion does not.
entries.why_then: Gibbon wrote in the Enlightenment, read the Latin and Greek historians closely, and had no archaeology, coin finds or economic data; moral and religious explanations were the natural frame of the history of his age.

match: The clergy successfully preached the doctrines of patience and pusillanimity
entries.modern: Few historians now hold that Christianity sapped Rome's military strength: the Eastern empire was at least as Christian and survived until 1453, and Christian emperors fought constantly. The Church is seen instead as one of the institutions that carried Roman administration and learning through the transition.
sources: Peter Brown, The Rise of Western Christendom (1996; 3rd ed. 2013)
A. H. M. Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284–602 (1964)
entries.relationship: A famous thesis of the book, now set aside.
entries.why_then: Gibbon shared the Enlightenment's suspicion of the clergy (as Voltaire did), and the monks and bishops of his Latin sources were vivid, the economics behind them invisible.

entries.topic: The size of the empire under the Antonines
match: empire was above two thousand miles in breadth
entries.modern: At its greatest extent (c. AD 117, under Trajan) the empire covered about 5 million km² — roughly 1.9 million square miles.
sources: Rein Taagepera, 'Size and Duration of Empires', Social Science History 3 (1979)
entries.relationship: Gibbon's figure ('above sixteen hundred thousand square miles') is about 15% below the modern estimate — close, for an estimate made from 18th-century maps.

match: about twice as many provincials as there were citizens
entries.modern: Modern demographers estimate the empire's population at about 45 million under Augustus and 60–75 million at its peak in the mid-2nd century, before the Antonine plague (from 165).
sources: Bruce W. Frier, 'Demography', Cambridge Ancient History vol. XI (2000)
Walter Scheidel, 'Demography', Cambridge Economic History of the Greco-Roman World (2007)
entries.relationship: Gibbon's 120 million is about twice the modern estimate; he reasoned from census figures for citizens without the age and survival data used today.

match: The precise year in which the Western empire was extinguished
entries.modern: AD 476 is the conventional date: Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople. Some historians prefer 480, the death of Julius Nepos, the last emperor recognised by the East.
sources: Peter Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
entries.relationship: Gibbon's caution that the year is 'not positively ascertained' matches modern debate over 476 versus 480.

entries.modern: Constantinople fell to the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II on 29 May 1453, after a siege of about seven weeks; the last emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting.
sources: Steven Runciman, The Fall of Constantinople 1453 (1965)
Marios Philippides & Walter Hanak, The Siege and the Fall of Constantinople in 1453 (2011)

match: real efficacy of the Greek fire
entries.modern: Greek fire, introduced about 672 (attributed to the engineer Kallinikos), was a petroleum-based incendiary projected through siphons; it did help save Constantinople in the Arab sieges of 674–678 and 717–718. Its exact recipe is still unknown.
sources: John Haldon, '“Greek fire” revisited', in Byzantine Style, Religion and Civilization (2006)
entries.relationship: Confirmed; the composition remains the mystery Gibbon described.
